James Pilkington
jāmz pil'king-ton
n. (James Pilkington, c. 1520–1576, bishop of Durham, the first Protestant to hold that see)
Hebrew Yaaqob, a supplanter, through Latin Jacobus; English Pilkington, from a Lancashire place-name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

James Pilkington was master of St John's College, Cambridge, an exile at Zurich, Basel and Geneva under Mary, and from 1561 the first Protestant bishop of Durham — the hardest diocese in England to reform, conservative, remote, and in 1569 the centre of the Northern Rising, during which the rebels restored the mass in Durham cathedral and Pilkington had to leave the county. He wrote commentaries on Haggai, Obadiah and Nehemiah, and they are the most interesting thing he left: all three are Old Testament books about rebuilding a ruined house of God in a hostile province, and he preached them to a diocese in precisely that condition. He founded the grammar school at Rivington in his native Lancashire, endowed it himself, and it survives. His sermons complain steadily about the poverty of the northern clergy and the pillaging of church revenues by gentlemen. “Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste” (Neh 2:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines see as the seat of episcopal power, a diocese, and rising as an insurrection, a tumultuous assembly.

SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.

RI'SING, n. The act of getting up; an insurrection; a tumultuous assembly.

COMMEN'TARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; an exposition of a book.

ENDOW', v. To enrich with a permanent fund or property; to settle a provision upon.

Key Scripture

Neh 2:17 — "Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach."

Neh 4:6 — "So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work."

Hag 1:4 — "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?"

Hag 2:4 — "Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, saith the LORD; and be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest; and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you, saith the LORD of hosts:"

Modern Corruption

Durham's first Protestant bishop, preaching Haggai and Nehemiah to a province in ruins.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a reading of the Northern Rising of 1569 as a popular revolt against an alien religion imposed from London, which is how it is often presented and which contains just enough truth to mislead. The north was conservative and the imposition was real. The rising was also led by two earls with dynastic ambitions, it restored the mass by force of arms, and it was crushed with several hundred hangings that did the Protestant cause in the north no good at all.

The principle to recover is the one Pilkington chose to preach, which is that rebuilding is slow, resisted, and commanded anyway. Nehemiah states the condition honestly before he states the task: “Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste” (Neh 2:17). Haggai rebukes the inverted priorities that leave the house waste: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). And then the encouragement with its reason attached: “be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you” (Hag 2:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew banah (H1129), to build, to rebuild; chazaq (H2388), to be strong, to take courage.

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build, to rebuild, to establish; Nehemiah 2:17.

Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, scorn, disgrace; Nehemiah 2:17.

Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the mind, the will; Nehemiah 4:6.

Hebrew charab (H2717) — to be waste, to be desolate; Haggai 1:4.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to take courage, to prevail; Haggai 2:4.

Usage

"“Ye see the distress that we are in” (Neh 2:17) — Durham, 1561."

"“this house lie waste” (Hag 1:4) — against the pillagers of church revenue."

"“be strong, all ye people of the land” (Hag 2:4) — the school at Rivington, endowed and standing."
